key_terms.meaning: Data kept as fixed-size blocks on a device that a server mounts like a local disk; the OS filesystem decides what the blocks mean, so latency is low but blocks are tied to one machine.
Data kept as named files inside folders on a shared server, reached over a network protocol such as NFS or SMB; the hierarchy is visible and the unit of access is the whole file or a byte range.
Data kept as whole objects, each with a unique key and its own metadata, in a flat namespace reached over HTTP; scales to billions of objects but you cannot edit a byte inside an object.
A fixed-size piece of a file (often 64 MB or 128 MB) that a distributed file system stores and replicates as one unit.
The data about the data — file name, size, chunk list, chunk locations, checksums, timestamps — kept small and in memory so lookups are fast.
The single HDFS master that holds the whole namespace and the chunk-to-server map in RAM, and hands out locations but never carries file data.
An HDFS worker that stores chunks on its local disk and serves read and write requests for those chunks.
The number of copies kept of each chunk, usually 3; durability improves as it rises, and storage cost rises in the same proportion.
A sparse, distributed, sorted map from (row key, column, timestamp) to a byte value, split into tablets and stored on many machines.
A named group of columns in BigTable that is stored together and compressed together; you design the table around families, not around individual columns.
A family of stores (key-value, column, document, graph) that drop joins and fixed schemas to spread data over thousands of machines.
Deciding how much capacity — how many hosts, VMs, vCPUs, GB of RAM and IOPS — to make available before any request arrives.
Million instructions per second, the unit CloudSim uses to state how much computing power a host gives a VM; a host of 1000 MIPS split 500/500 gives each of two VMs 500 MIPS.
Service level agreement: the promised response time, uptime and throughput, with penalties if the promise is broken; it is the limit inside which utilisation may rise.
The fixed machinery of a scheduler — the run queue, the timer interrupt, the context switch, the dispatcher — which stays the same whatever rule is chosen.
The replaceable rule that picks which ready item runs next, such as FIFO, round robin, shortest job first or a cost-aware rule.
The CloudSim name for one unit of work (a task with length in million instructions) that is placed in a VM and executed.
Recovery time objective: the longest time the service may be down after a failure before the promise is broken, for example 15 minutes.
Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling: lowering a chip's clock and supply voltage when load is light, cutting power roughly with the cube of the voltage.
An arrangement where independent cloud providers agree on interfaces so that capacity can be lent and borrowed and one job can run across both.

takeaways: Splitting a file into chunks with metadata is what lets a cloud place it on thousands of cheap disks, and that split is what fixes durability, latency and cost.
GFS and HDFS both keep one master holding only metadata and many workers holding three replicas of every chunk, so a dead disk is repaired from a surviving copy.
BigTable is a sorted sparse map indexed by row key, column and timestamp; its order makes range scans cheap and its sparsity means empty cells cost nothing.
Provisioning sizes the pool of capacity, allocation hands each request to a host or VM, and the score of both is the gap between utilisation and the SLA.
Splitting a scheduler into mechanism and policy lets a provider trade fairness for throughput by changing a rule, not by rebuilding the queue and dispatcher.
Fault tolerance is designed, not hoped for: assume failure, detect it, move work to a replica, and state the recovery time and data-loss window.
Idle servers still draw most of their peak power, so consolidation with live migration and DVFS attack the power bill that dominates data-centre cost.
A cloud is a market: published prices, bids from users and brokers, a scheduler matching demand to supply, and a bill that is metered usage times unit price.
Federation lets one job use two providers' capacity through agreed interfaces; multi-cloud means using several providers without any such agreement, and hybrid means mixing private and public.
bank_note: Long answers in this unit are rewarded for showing the design trade-off — why the architecture is shaped that way, what it costs, and where it breaks — rather than for listing component names.

bank.q: Compare block, file and object storage on the unit of access, the protocol used, typical latency and cost per GB, and give one cloud workload that fits each.
outline: Block: raw fixed-size blocks over iSCSI or a virtual disk attach; lowest latency; used for databases and boot volumes.
File: named files in folders over NFS or SMB; shared access with locking; used for home directories and general shared content.
Object: flat key-value namespace over HTTP, metadata travels with each object; highest throughput per object but no in-place edits; used for backups, images, logs.
Rule of thumb: latency and control fall from block to file to object; scale and cost per GB rise in the other direction.
State that no single type wins; the access pattern decides.

bank.q: Explain the GFS/HDFS architecture and trace one file write and one file read through it.
outline: One master holds namespace and chunk map in RAM; many chunk servers hold chunks on local disk, typically 64 MB each.
Client asks the master for chunk locations; master replies with a list of servers ordered by network distance.
Write: client is given a lease holder, data flows along a pipeline of replicas, and success is acknowledged only when all replicas have the chunk.
Read: client contacts the nearest replica directly; the master is not in the data path, so throughput scales with the number of servers.
Every chunk has three copies on different racks; heartbeats let the master detect a dead server and re-replicate.
Why this shape: commodity disks fail often, so software replication is cheaper than expensive hardware; large sequential reads dominate the workload.

bank.q: Describe BigTable as a data model. Explain row key, column family, timestamp and sparsity, and why rows are kept in sorted order.
outline: Model is a map: (row key, column, timestamp) → byte string; nothing else is assumed about the value.
Rows are sorted lexicographically by row key and split into tablets that migrate between servers.
Column families are created up front and stored and compressed together; new columns inside a family need no schema change.
Timestamps keep several versions of a cell; garbage collection keeps the last n or the last t seconds.
Sparsity: absent cells take no space, so a very wide table is normal.
Sorted order makes range scans by key prefix cheap — the design reason for reversing the domain in row keys so that related items sit together.

bank.q: Distinguish resource provisioning from resource allocation. Define MIPS and show how MIPS is used to decide whether a host can hold one more VM.
outline: Provisioning: deciding total capacity and making it available ahead of time (hosts, VMs, storage, network).
Allocation: at request time, choosing which host or VM serves this request.
MIPS = million instructions per second; a host has total MIPS and total RAM, and each VM asks for a share.
Feasibility test: sum of allocated MIPS ≤ host MIPS and sum of allocated RAM ≤ host RAM, plus bandwidth and storage checks.
Oversized provisioning wastes money; undersized provisioning overruns the SLA; the aim is minimum slack consistent with the SLA.

bank.q: Define scheduling policy and scheduling mechanism, and show how a provider changes one without rebuilding the other.
outline: Mechanism: run queue, timer interrupt, context switch, dispatcher — the part that actually moves work onto a CPU or VM.
Policy: the rule that selects the next ready item — FIFO, round robin, shortest job first, priority, cost-aware.
Same mechanism can run any policy: the queue and dispatcher are unchanged, only the pick function is replaced.
Example: switching from round robin to shortest-job-first raises throughput but can starve long jobs; the mechanism is untouched.
In CloudSim, the broker and the VM scheduler hold the mechanism and the allocation policy is the pluggable part.

bank.q: A 640 MB file is stored with 64 MB chunks and replication factor 3. Compute how many chunks exist in the namespace, how much raw disk is used, and what the system does when one chunk server dies.
outline: Chunks in namespace = 640 ÷ 64 = 10.
Raw disk = 10 × 64 MB × 3 = 1920 MB, i.e. 1.875 GB for a 640 MB file.
Loss of one server loses at most one replica of some chunks; the master sees missing heartbeats and schedules re-replication.
Re-replication copies from a surviving replica to a new server until the factor is 3 again; reads continue throughout.
Note the overhead ratio 3:1, and that a smaller chunk size would raise the metadata burden on the NameNode.

bank.q: A service has 10 identical hosts, each carrying 8 VMs of 1000 MIPS. Demand over 24 hours is given in a table. Show how consolidation with live migration reduces the number of powered hosts, and check the SLA after consolidation.
outline: Compute total MIPS demanded in each interval and divide by host capacity to get the minimum host count.
Compare with the always-on 10-host baseline: the difference is the idle capacity that consolidation removes.
Live migration moves a VM with a short pause; it costs network bandwidth and a little CPU on both ends, so migrate during a trough.
Check SLA: after consolidation no host should exceed a safe utilisation ceiling, because queueing delay grows sharply near 100 percent.
Compute power saved as (hosts removed) × idle power, then add the saving from DVFS on the surviving hosts.
State the risk: too aggressive consolidation leaves no headroom for a sudden spike; keep a reserve.

bank.q: Three providers publish prices and a broker has a job with a deadline. Describe how the broker chooses a provider and how the final bill is computed.
outline: List each provider's unit price (per VM-hour or per million instructions), startup delay and transfer cost.
Filter providers that can meet the deadline and the SLA; among the rest, rank by total cost.
Total cost = compute units × unit price + storage GB-month + data transfer out + any minimum charge.
Billing granularity matters: per-second billing and per-hour rounding can differ by a large factor for short jobs.
Add the broker's own fee; state who bears the risk if the job overruns the deadline.
Mention spot or bid-based pricing: cheaper, but the instance can be withdrawn, so it suits tolerant batch work only.

bank.q: Design fault tolerance for a service that promises RTO of 15 minutes and RPO of 5 minutes. State the replication, detection and failover steps.
outline: RTO = 15 min: longest allowed downtime; RPO = 5 min: most data that may be lost, measured in time.
Replication: three copies across racks, plus asynchronous cross-region copy every few minutes to bound RPO.
Detection: heartbeats and health checks at a stated interval; a slow detector inflates RTO, a fast one risks false failover.
Failover: health check fails → traffic switched by DNS or load balancer to the standby → standby promoted, writes resume.
Data: replay the write-ahead log or transaction log; async replication means the last few minutes may need replay, which is exactly the RPO.
Test the whole path on a schedule: an untested failover is a guess. Record the measured RTO and RPO afterwards.

bank.q: A batch job must run in two different clouds owned by different providers. Explain what a third-party broker does, step by step, from submission to billing.
outline: User submits the job and constraints to the broker, not to either provider.
Broker translates the job into each provider's API through the agreed federation interface.
Broker splits the work, places parts according to price, capacity and data location, and moves input data or reads it where it already sits.
Broker monitors progress, restarts failed parts on the other cloud, and enforces the SLA.
Broker returns one consolidated bill and one status view; the user never opens two accounts.
Trust and data-protection terms are agreed between providers in advance, which is what separates federation from ad-hoc multi-cloud.

bank.q: Analyse why GFS and HDFS use a single metadata master. What breaks first as the cluster grows, and what are the mitigations?
outline: Single master keeps the namespace consistent without distributed locking and keeps lookups in RAM, so latency is tiny.
It removes the master from the data path, so read throughput scales with the number of chunk servers, not with master size.
Bottleneck is master RAM: roughly a few hundred bytes per file and per chunk, so billions of small files exhaust it.
Second bottleneck is the write path: every new chunk needs a master decision, so creation rate, not bandwidth, saturates.
Mitigations: larger chunk size, fewer small files by packing, a read-only shadow master, and federation of namespaces.
Newer designs split the namespace across many masters with a table layer; note that they give up the simple single-lock model.
Judgement: the design is right for a few large files read sequentially, wrong for a social-media photo store, where object storage wins.

bank.q: Evaluate the trade-off between energy saving and SLA compliance in a green data centre. Use PUE, idle power and DVFS in your answer, and recommend a policy.
outline: PUE = total facility power ÷ IT equipment power; a PUE of 1.2 means 20 percent overhead. Lower is better and free cooling is the main lever.
Idle servers draw a large fraction of peak power, so many lightly loaded hosts waste far more than one busy host.
Consolidation plus live migration raises utilisation and cuts the number of powered hosts, but leaves less headroom for spikes.
DVFS cuts power roughly with the cube of voltage; it helps only when the workload is not memory-latency bound.
Renewable-aware scheduling shifts deferrable batch work to hours when the grid is clean; interactive work cannot be shifted.
Recommendation: consolidate to a safe ceiling, keep a small reserve, use migration only in troughs, and put deferrable jobs where and when energy is cheapest and cleanest.
State the metric that decides: energy per completed request at a stated SLA percentile, not energy alone.

bank.q: A team must store 10 million files of about 100 KB each. Evaluate HDFS, object storage and BigTable for this workload and justify a choice.
outline: HDFS: one metadata entry per file and per chunk in NameNode RAM; 10 million small files is a memory problem, and a 64 MB block wastes space on a 100 KB file.
HDFS read path is built for long sequential reads; many tiny reads mean one master lookup per file — latency dominated by metadata.
Object storage: flat namespace, per-object metadata held by the store, scales to billions of keys, HTTP access, no in-place edits.
BigTable or a key-value store: good when the file is looked up by key and you want ordered scans by key prefix, and when values are small.
Decision rule: size of the object, need for in-place update, need for range scans by key, cost per GB and per request.
Recommendation for a photo or document store: object storage with a database index; keep HDFS for large sequential analytical files.

bank.q: "Federation, hybrid cloud and multi-cloud are not the same thing." Analyse the differences in interfaces, billing, trust and failure handling, and say when federation is worth the cost.
outline: Multi-cloud: one user, several providers, no agreement between them; the user integrates everything and bills separately.
Hybrid: private infrastructure plus one public provider, joined by a secure link and a common management layer.
Federation: providers publish agreed interfaces and lend capacity; a broker can place one job across two clouds.
Interfaces: federation needs a common API, identity and data-movement standard; multi-cloud needs only per-provider SDKs.
Billing: federation can produce one bill through a broker; multi-cloud produces as many bills as providers.
Trust: federation requires agreed data-protection and jurisdiction terms before any job runs; multi-cloud leaves this to the user.
Failure handling: in federation the broker can restart a failed part elsewhere; without it the user's own orchestrator must.
Worth it when peak demand exceeds one provider's capacity or when price differences are large and the job is portable; not worth it for a single short-lived workload.

glossary.def: A fixed-size slice of a file that a distributed file system stores, replicates and checksums as one unit.
The HDFS master process that holds the file namespace and chunk locations in memory.
An HDFS worker process that stores chunks on local disk and serves reads and writes.
The tree of file and directory names plus their attributes, kept by the master separately from the data itself.
A periodic short message from a worker to the master saying it is alive; missed heartbeats trigger re-replication.
The number of copies kept of each chunk, three by default in GFS and HDFS.
A contiguous sorted range of BigTable rows that is the unit of distribution and migration.
A named set of BigTable columns stored and compressed together, created when the table is created.
A table in which missing cells take no storage, so very wide tables are practical.
The guarantee about what a reader sees after a write; strong consistency makes replicas agree before replying.
A software-defined computer with its own vCPUs, RAM and disk, running on a shared physical host.
The layer that runs virtual machines and divides physical CPU, memory and I/O among them.
Moving a running VM to another host with a pause short enough that users do not notice.
Million instructions per second, the capacity unit CloudSim uses for hosts, VMs and tasks.
Making capacity available ahead of demand, in hosts, VMs, storage and network.
Choosing the host or VM that will actually serve a given request or task.
The mechanism component that performs the context switch and puts the chosen item on the processor.
In CloudSim, one task with a length in million instructions and a file size, placed in a VM.
The component that accepts a user's request, chooses resources under a policy and submits tasks to them.
The property that the service keeps meeting its promise when a component fails, using detection, redundancy and recovery.
Recovery time objective, the longest allowed downtime after a failure.
Recovery point objective, the largest amount of data, measured as time, that may be lost in a failure.
Power usage effectiveness: total facility power divided by IT equipment power; 1.0 is perfect.
Dynamic voltage and frequency scaling, lowering clock speed and voltage when load falls to cut power.
Capacity sold at a discount that the provider may reclaim at short notice, suited to tolerant batch work.
The idea of a fabric of interconnected clouds that can exchange capacity and move workloads between each other.
